summary: Defines a Management Information Base module for managing a ForCES network element. It provides managed objects used with network management protocols such as SNMP. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a checklist of dials and gauges so a manager can look at and adjust a ForCES device.

questions: which snmp objects does forces define
subtitle: A read-only SNMP MIB that lets managers see which ForCES control and forwarding elements are associated and how busy they are.

tldr.problem: Operators of a ForCES network element need a standard way to see which Control Elements and Forwarding Elements are currently associated, and with which protocol version.
tldr.mechanism: A read-only SMIv2 MIB module, FORCES-MIB, holds a table with one row per association that is UP, plus notifications when associations come up or go down.
tldr.outcome: Managers can monitor ForCES associations over SNMP without being able to change anything. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 5813 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The ForCES MIB module is a read-only MIB module that captures information about the ForCES protocol, which separates the Control Elements (CEs) from the Forwarding Elements (FEs) of a Network Element (NE). It follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework and is written in SMIv2, so its objects are generally read over SNMP.

It leaves out information that other MIB modules already cover, such as packet counters for interfaces. For associations between CEs and FEs that are in the UP state, it provides three kinds of information: the identifiers of the elements, configuration parameters of the association, and statistics of the association.
sections.eli5: A big machine has a brain part and a muscle part that talk to each other. This document lists the gauges that show whether they are talking.

sections.title: What the Module Reports
sections.content:
The module holds the latest ForCES protocol version the CE supports (forcesLatestProtocolVersionSupported). The CE must still allow interaction with FEs that support earlier versions.

For each association, identified by the pair of CE ID and FE ID, one entry in forcesAssociationTable provides:

  • the protocol version running in the association;
  • the time the association entered the UP state, and the time it left it (the latter is used for notifications only);
  • counts of Heartbeat messages sent and received by the CE since the association came up;
  • counts of operational messages sent and received. Heartbeat, Association Setup, Association Setup Response and Association Teardown messages are not counted as operational.

There are also notifications. forcesAssociationEntryUp and forcesAssociationEntryDown carry the running protocol version. Optional ...UpStats and ...DownStats variants carry the associated statistics instead.
sections.eli5: For each pair of connected parts, the dashboard shows what language they speak, when they connected, and how many messages they have swapped. It also rings a bell when a pair connects or disconnects.

sections.title: The MIB Definition
sections.content:
The module is FORCES-MIB, registered as { mib-2 187 }. It defines two textual conventions: ForcesID, a 4-octet quantity, and ForcesProtocolVersion, an integer from 1 to 255, where 1 means ForCESv1 (RFC 5810).

Rows of forcesAssociationTable are indexed by forcesAssociationCEID and forcesAssociationFEID. Each row also has the running protocol version, forcesAssociationTimeUp, forcesAssociationTimeDown, four zero-based counters (Heartbeat and operational messages, sent and received) and forcesAssociationCounterDiscontinuityTime.

The time-up value is the sysUpTime when the association entered UP, and it uniquely identifies associations that share the same CE and FE IDs. The discontinuity time records when any counter of the association last suffered a discontinuity, or is zero if none has.
sections.eli5: Every connected pair gets one row in a big table, labeled with the two names. The row holds the numbers: when they connected, how many messages went each way, and when the counters were last reset.

sections.title: Which Associations Appear
sections.content:
An association enters the UP state as soon as the CE has sent the FE an Association Setup Response message containing a successful Association Setup Result. Only UP associations are shown in the MIB.

An association is removed from the MIB as soon as it leaves UP. That happens if the CE receives no message from the FE (Heartbeat or other) within a given time period, or if the CE sends an Association Teardown message.

Counters start at zero when the association is created. If the same association goes down and comes back up, the counters reset, and the discontinuity timestamp shows it. The optional down notification carries the final values of the counters. The notifications are not throttled, because the CE itself should throttle the setup of associations.

With more than one CE, information about associations may be spread across the CEs. Whether each CE reports its own or they cooperate to show one set of objects is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: A pair only shows on the dashboard while it is really connected. When it disconnects its row disappears, and if it reconnects the counters start again at zero.

sections.title: Compliance and Object Groups
sections.content:
The compliance statement says that implementations MUST support two groups. forcesMibGroup holds the latest supported protocol version and the running protocol version. forcesNotificationGroup holds the basic up and down notifications.

Two further groups are recommended. forcesStatsGroup holds the optional timestamps and counters, which the RFC says have no protocol reason to be kept but can be very useful in debugging connectivity problems. forcesNotificationStatsGroup holds the notifications that include statistics.
sections.eli5: Some gauges are required on every device. Others are nice extras that help you work out why two parts cannot talk.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in the module has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, so if the module is implemented correctly an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through SNMP SET operations.

Readable objects may still be sensitive in some environments, so access to GET and NOTIFY should be controlled, and values may need to be encrypted in transit. The RFC judges the objects in forcesMibGroup (protocol versions) and forcesStatsGroup (statistics) to be neither sensitive nor vulnerable.

It RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says that deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: You cannot change anything through this dashboard, only look. Even so, only the right people should be allowed to look, and SNMPv3 is the safer way to let them.

items.label: forcesAssociationEntryUp
items.desc: An association entered the UP state; carries the running protocol version.

items.label: forcesAssociationEntryDown
items.desc: An association left the UP state; carries the running protocol version.

items.label: forcesAssociationEntryUpStats
items.desc: Optional UP notification that adds the time-up value.

items.label: forcesAssociationEntryDownStats
items.desc: Optional DOWN notification with times and the final counter values.
